summary: Defines the revised IDNA protocol for registering and looking up internationalized domain names without changing the DNS itself. It is meant only for domain names, not free text. It is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 3490 and RFC 3491.

plainLanguage.summary: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) lets people use non-ASCII characters in domain names while leaving DNS itself unchanged. Applications validate a Unicode label and encode it as an ASCII-compatible label beginning with xn-- for DNS registration and lookup.

subtitle: Defines how applications register and look up domain names that contain non-ASCII labels.

tldr.problem: DNS uses ASCII labels, but people and organizations need domain names that can use characters from other writing systems.
tldr.mechanism: IDNA2008 validates Unicode labels and converts them to ASCII-compatible Punycode labels with the prefix xn-- before DNS registration or lookup.
tldr.outcome: Applications can handle internationalized domain names without changing DNS servers or the DNS protocol. RFC 5891 obsoletes RFCs 3490 and 3491 and updates RFC 3492.

today: RFC 5891 is a Proposed Standard defining the IDNA2008 protocol. It obsoletes RFC 3490 and RFC 3491, and updates RFC 3492.

sections.title: Internationalized Names on an ASCII DNS
sections.content:
IDNA2008 defines how applications register and look up internationalized domain names. It applies only to domain names, not to arbitrary text, and does not require changes to DNS servers, resolvers, or DNS messages.

It works by representing eligible non-ASCII labels with special ASCII labels. Older protocols that are not IDNA-aware must use the ASCII-compatible form when carrying these names.
sections.plainLanguage: IDNA lets a domain name include characters beyond ASCII without changing how DNS works. An application converts the name into an ASCII form before using DNS.

sections.title: Registering a Domain Label
sections.content:
For registration, the input must be Unicode in Normalization Form C. The registry checks that characters are allowed, that the label meets the hyphen and combining-mark rules, and that contextual and right-to-left requirements are satisfied.

The registry may apply additional local restrictions. After validation, the label is converted to an ASCII-compatible label using Punycode with the prefix xn--, and that ASCII label is inserted into the DNS zone.
sections.plainLanguage: Registration checks that a proposed Unicode label follows IDNA's character and label rules. A valid label is converted into an ASCII-compatible form before it is stored in DNS.

sections.title: Looking Up a Domain Name
sections.content:
Lookup begins with a name supplied by a user or another application and converts it to Unicode NFC if needed. An application that receives an apparent A-label beginning with xn-- may decode it and check that the result matches the original label.

The lookup checks reject malformed, disallowed, unassigned, or improperly contextualized labels. The valid label is encoded as an A-label, combined with the other domain labels, and resolved using normal DNS procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a lookup, the application checks the label and converts it to the same ASCII-compatible form used in DNS. DNS then resolves the full name through its usual process.

sections.title: Unicode Labels and Punycode
sections.content:
A U-label is a valid Unicode label containing at least one non-ASCII character. Its A-label form is produced by applying the Punycode algorithm and adding the ASCII Compatible Encoding prefix xn--.

Domain names used directly in DNS queries or responses must use A-labels. IDNA-aware protocols may accept U-labels, A-labels, or both, according to their own specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The Unicode spelling is converted to an ASCII spelling that starts with xn--. DNS uses this encoded spelling, while an IDNA-aware application can show the Unicode form to a user.

sections.title: Validation and Confusable Names
sections.content:
Internationalized labels can be visually confused with other names or rendered unexpectedly. The RFC expects registries to define careful policies about which labels they accept, including rules that can depend on the label's characters and other registered labels.

Labels that use right-to-left scripts must follow the applicable bidirectional rules. The protocol validates labels but does not remove the need for responsible registry policies or careful application display.
sections.plainLanguage: Different characters can look alike, and mixed writing directions can make names hard to read. Registries and applications need to apply the label rules and present names carefully.
